newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bankruptcy debt up nearly 50% in Nov yr/yr.
newsitem.headline: Japan bankruptcy debt up nearly 50% in Nov yr/yr.

text.p: Total debt held by bankrupt firms in Japan jumped 49.6 percent in November from the same month a year earlier to 1.55 trillion yen, a private research and rating company said on Friday.

The surge in debt was mainly due to a series of failures triggered by the lingering effects of the end of the economic bubble of inflated land and stock prices in late 1980s, Tokyo Commerce and Industry Research Co said in a report.
The failures included major realtor Sueno Kosan, which collapsed with debts of about 716 billion yen, the second-largest insolvency case in Japan since World War Two, the report said.
Sueno, based in Osaka, borrowed heavily from failed "jusen" mortgage firms. Total debts of Sueno and its two group firms were 975 billion yen, the report said.
Large-scale bankruptcy cases involving total debts of more than one billion yen surged to 75 in November from October's 48.
The number of companies filing for bankruptcy in Japan in November rose 6.8 percent from a year earlier to 1,339.
More than half of the cases were caused by weak economic conditions, the report said.
Of such cases, 614 failures were due to sluggish sales, 157 failures were due to accumulated losses and 32 failures were caused by trouble collecting money owed, the report said.
"The number of corporate failures, especially among small- and medium-sized companies, continues to be at a high level amid changes in the industrial structure," Tokyo Commerce said.
The outlook is equally bleak. The credit research firm said that there are even some signs that the economy is falling back into a recession.

"Consumption activities are becoming increasingly restrained in light of the expected increases in the sales tax and utility charges as well as due to uncertainty in the outlook for incomes," Tokyo Commerce said.
It also said that public works projects will likely no longer provide strong support to the economy, while private sector capital outlays remain generally sluggish.
In November, the number of bankruptcies in the service sector was up 18.3 percent from a year ago to 161, and those in the construction sector rose 12.6 percent to 365.
Bankruptcies in the real estate sector, meanwhile, fell 28.1 percent from a year earlier to 46 cases.
Tokyo Commerce expects that the number of failures in 1996 will total around 14,950, down from 15,108 last year, but up from 14,061 in 1994.
